questions.question: What is a 'user' in Linux?

options.text: A person physically sitting at the computer
An account that allows someone or something to log in and use system resources
A program running in the background

explanation.correct: A user in Linux is an account — a named identity that allows someone or something to log into the system and access resources like files, commands, and processes.
explanation.why: A is incorrect because system users are not humans. C describes processes. D is about permissions, not users.

questions.question: What is the UID of the root user on any Linux system?

explanation.correct: The root user always has UID 0. This is consistent across all Linux distributions and versions.
explanation.why: UID 0 is reserved exclusively for root. UIDs 1–999 are for system users, and 1000+ are for normal users.

questions.question: Which file stores the encrypted passwords for user accounts in Linux?

explanation.correct: /etc/shadow stores encrypted passwords and is readable only by root. /etc/passwd stores basic user info but shows 'x' where the password used to be.
explanation.why: Originally /etc/passwd held passwords, but they were moved to /etc/shadow for security because /etc/passwd is world-readable.

questions.question: What is the UID range for normal user accounts in Linux?

explanation.correct: Normal (human) user accounts have UIDs of 1000 and above on modern Linux systems.
explanation.why: UIDs 0 is root, 1–999 are for system/service accounts. Normal users start from 1000.

questions.question: Which command is used to create a new user in Linux?

explanation.correct: useradd is the standard command to create a new user account in Linux. It requires sudo privileges.
explanation.why: adduser exists on some distributions (like Ubuntu) as a friendlier wrapper, but useradd is the standard utility across all Linux distributions.

questions.question: What does the -r flag do when used with userdel?

options.text: Removes the user's home directory along with the account
Runs the command recursively on all users

explanation.correct: userdel -r username deletes the user account AND removes their home directory. Without -r, the home directory is left behind.
explanation.why: This is an important distinction — userdel alone does not clean up the /home/username folder.

questions.question: Which file contains basic information about all user accounts, including their UID and home directory?

explanation.correct: /etc/passwd contains basic info about every user: username, UID, GID, home directory, and default shell. It is readable by all users.
explanation.why: /etc/shadow has encrypted passwords (root only), /etc/group has group info.

questions.question: What does the id command show when you run 'id vikram'?

options.text: The UID, primary GID, and all group memberships of vikram
The last login time for vikram

explanation.correct: id username shows the user's UID (uid=), primary group GID (gid=), and all groups they belong to (groups=).
explanation.why: This is the key command to verify user and group management changes.

questions.question: Which command safely edits the /etc/sudoers file?

explanation.correct: visudo should always be used to edit /etc/sudoers because it validates the syntax before saving. A typo in sudoers can lock you out of sudo entirely.
explanation.why: Never edit /etc/sudoers with a regular text editor — a syntax error can prevent all sudo access.

questions.question: Which group must a normal user belong to in order to use sudo on Amazon Linux?

explanation.correct: On Amazon Linux, CentOS, and RHEL, the wheel group grants sudo access to normal users.
explanation.why: Ubuntu and Debian use a group called 'sudo' instead. Knowing this difference is important when working across Linux distributions.

questions.question: What is the correct command to add vikram to the developers group WITHOUT removing existing group memberships?

explanation.correct: usermod -aG appends the new group to the user's existing group memberships. The -a flag means 'append', the -G flag specifies secondary groups.
explanation.why: Without -a, the -G flag replaces ALL secondary groups with just the one specified.

questions.question: Where is the SSH public key stored for the ec2-user on an Amazon Linux EC2 instance?

explanation.correct: The public key for SSH authentication is stored at ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — inside the user's home directory, in a hidden .ssh folder.
explanation.why: This is why SSH key authentication is user-specific. The private key on your laptop is matched against this file.

questions.question: What happens when you run 'sudo usermod -G developers vikram' (WITHOUT the -a flag)?

options.text: Adds developers as an additional group, keeping all existing groups
Creates a new group called developers
Replaces ALL of vikram's secondary groups with just developers

explanation.correct: Without the -a (append) flag, -G replaces all secondary group memberships. If vikram was in wheel, docker, and qa, all those memberships are lost — only developers remains.
explanation.why: This is one of the most common mistakes in user management. Always use -aG unless you intentionally want to replace all groups.

questions.question: What is the difference between a primary group and a secondary group?

options.text: Primary groups are more powerful than secondary groups
Primary group is created automatically with the user and is used for new file ownership; secondary groups are additional groups for permissions
Secondary groups are for root users only

explanation.correct: The primary group (same name as user, created automatically) is assigned to new files the user creates. Secondary groups are additional group memberships used for accessing shared resources.
explanation.why: When a user creates a file, the file's group ownership defaults to the user's primary group.

questions.question: A user has UID 72. Which type of user is this?

explanation.correct: UIDs 1–999 are reserved for system users and service accounts. UID 72 falls in this range, so it is a system/service account created by Linux for a background service.
explanation.why: Normal users start at UID 1000. You can quickly identify user types just by looking at their UID.

questions.question: What is sudo short for, and what is its main purpose?

options.text: System User Delete Operation — removes user accounts
Superuser Do — runs a command with root privileges temporarily
Switch User Directory — changes home directory
Secure Unix Domain Operation — encrypts files

explanation.correct: sudo stands for 'superuser do'. It lets a normal user run a single command with root privileges without actually switching to the root account.
explanation.why: This is safer than logging in as root because the elevated privilege is limited to just that one command.

questions.question: Which command switches to another user AND loads their complete environment (home directory, PATH, etc.)?

explanation.correct: su - username (with the hyphen/dash) switches to the user and fully loads their environment — home directory, PATH, shell settings, etc. su username without the hyphen only changes the user identity.
explanation.why: The hyphen in 'su -' simulates a full login. Without it, environment variables from the previous user session may persist.

questions.question: What port number does SSH use by default?

explanation.correct: SSH uses port 22 by default. This is why when launching EC2 instances, the security group needs to allow inbound traffic on port 22 for SSH access.
explanation.why: Port 80 is HTTP, 443 is HTTPS, 3389 is RDP (Windows Remote Desktop).

questions.question: What is the purpose of system users in Linux?

options.text: They are superuser accounts created by the admin
They are accounts created by the system itself to run background services; they cannot be used for login
They are temporary guest accounts for visitors
They are backups of normal user accounts

explanation.correct: System users (service accounts) are created automatically by Linux or software installations (like Docker, Apache) to run specific background services. They have no login capability.
explanation.why: This is a security design — each service runs as an isolated account. If one service is compromised, the attacker cannot easily pivot to other services.

questions.question: On an Ubuntu server, which group grants a normal user sudo access?

explanation.correct: On Ubuntu and Debian, the sudo group grants sudo access. On Amazon Linux, CentOS, and RHEL, the equivalent group is called wheel.
explanation.why: This is a distribution-specific difference you must know — adding to wheel works on RHEL-based systems, adding to sudo works on Debian-based systems.

questions.question: Which of the following /etc/passwd entries represents a root user?

explanation.correct: The root user entry has UID 0 and GID 0 with home directory /root. The third and fourth fields (UID:GID) are both 0, which is the definitive identifier for root.
explanation.why: A has UID 1000 (normal user), C has UID 74 (system user), D has UID 48 (system user).

questions.question: What does the /sbin/nologin shell in /etc/passwd indicate about a user?

options.text: The user can only log in once per day
The user account exists but cannot be used for interactive login
The user must use a non-standard login method

explanation.correct: /sbin/nologin as the default shell means the account cannot be used for interactive login. This is typically set for system/service accounts that should never be logged into.
explanation.why: System users need to exist (to own processes and files) but should never allow login for security reasons.

questions.question: You need to verify whether vikram was successfully added to the docker group. Which command is most efficient?

explanation.correct: id vikram shows the user's UID, primary GID, and all current group memberships in one output. It is the fastest way to verify group membership.
explanation.why: cat /etc/passwd shows basic info but not secondary groups. /etc/group would also work but id is faster and shows everything at once.

questions.question: A user is accidentally deleted using userdel (without -r). The /home/username directory still exists. What is the correct command to remove it?

explanation.correct: rm -rf is needed because the home directory contains files (and hidden files). rmdir only works on empty directories. rm -rf forcefully removes the directory and all its contents recursively.
explanation.why: userdel -r won't work because the user account is already deleted. The -rf flags on rm mean: -r recursive (enter subdirectories), -f force (no confirmation).

questions.question: What is stored in the /etc/group file?

options.text: Only the list of system groups
All group names, their GIDs, and the list of users who belong to each group
Only the primary groups of each user

explanation.correct: /etc/group contains all group information: group name, group password (rarely used), GID, and comma-separated list of members. This is where secondary group memberships are recorded.
explanation.why: Primary group membership is also recorded in /etc/passwd (the GID field), but /etc/group is the definitive source for all group-to-user mappings.

questions.question: What is the effect of adding NOPASSWD:ALL to the sudoers file for a user?

options.text: The user can never use sudo
The user can run any sudo command without being prompted for a password
The user can only run commands as other normal users, not root
The user's password is removed from the system

explanation.correct: NOPASSWD:ALL in sudoers means the user can run any command with sudo without entering a password. This is configured for ec2-user on Amazon Linux EC2 instances by default.
explanation.why: While convenient, NOPASSWD should be used carefully. In production, password prompts add an important layer of security against accidental or unauthorised command execution.

questions.question: A sysadmin runs 'sudo usermod -g QA vikram'. What changes, and what remains the same?

options.text: Adds QA as a secondary group; primary group unchanged
Changes vikram's primary group to QA; secondary groups unchanged
Creates a new group called QA and adds vikram to it
Removes vikram from all groups and adds only QA

explanation.correct: usermod -g (lowercase) changes the user's PRIMARY group to QA. Secondary group memberships are not affected. This is different from -G (uppercase) which changes secondary groups.
explanation.why: Remember: -g = primary group, -G = secondary groups, -aG = append to secondary groups. The case of the flag matters significantly.

questions.question: Why does Linux not require antivirus software the way Windows does?

options.text: Linux has no viruses because it is open source
Linux has a granular file permission system where every file has read/write/execute controls per user and group, preventing unauthorised access
Linux is only used on servers, not desktop computers
Linux uses a different processor architecture that viruses cannot target

explanation.correct: Linux's file permission system (read, write, execute for user, group, others) controls access to every single file — including system files. This granular control prevents most unauthorized access without needing antivirus software.
explanation.why: This is a fundamental design difference. Each file has permission bits that restrict who can read, modify, or execute it.

questions.question: You install Docker on an Amazon Linux server. Which of the following automatically happens?

options.text: A new normal user called 'docker' is created with UID 1000+
The root user gets renamed to 'docker'
A system user and a group called 'docker' are created automatically by the installer
Docker shares the ec2-user account for its processes

explanation.correct: When Docker is installed, it automatically creates a system user account (UID in 1–999 range) and a group called 'docker'. Users added to this group can run Docker commands without sudo.
explanation.why: This is standard Linux practice — software creates its own service account and group for isolated, secure operation.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the security difference between 'su - root' and using 'sudo' for a specific command?

options.text: They are identical in terms of security
su - root gives a full interactive root session with unlimited access until you exit; sudo runs a single command as root and immediately returns to normal user
sudo is more dangerous because it bypasses the sudoers file
su - root requires the user's password while sudo requires the root password

explanation.correct: su - root gives you a complete root shell session — all subsequent commands run as root until you exit. sudo runs exactly one specified command as root, then returns. This makes sudo much safer for day-to-day use.
explanation.why: With su - root, any mistake, malicious script, or accidental command runs with full root power. With sudo, each privileged command requires deliberate invocation.
